html:
The Business Analyst (BA) is the hinge between a business that knows what it wants and a delivery team that knows how to build it. This phase defines the BA craft, walks through the delivery life cycle where the BA works, and maps the Salesforce ecosystem you will operate in as a professional. It closes by aligning the six knowledge areas of the Salesforce Certified Business Analyst (CBA) exam to the seventeen phases of this roadmap.

Learning Objectives

  • Explain what a Salesforce Business Analyst actually does across a delivery life cycle...
  • Describe the six stages of the delivery life cycle and the artifact that ends each one...
  • Articulate the translation role the BA plays between business and technology...
  • Describe the Salesforce multi-tenant cloud platform and its core CRM clouds...
  • Distinguish standard objects, custom objects, Flows, approval processes, and reports...
  • Apply the platform funnel (Requirements to Reporting) when exploring an ask...
  • List the artifacts a BA produces on a Salesforce project and who uses them...
  • Map the six CBA exam blueprint knowledge areas to the roadmap phases that teach them...

1. What a Salesforce Business Analyst Actually Does

A Salesforce BA listens to stakeholders, documents the current process, defines the future state, writes clear requirements, and verifies the delivered solution satisfies the business need. In one day you might run a 45-minute workshop, draft a to-be swimlane, turn a vague request into a testable requirement, and walk a developer through an edge case in an approval Flow.

The job is fundamentally translation. Stakeholders speak in outcomes ("leads must move faster"), developers speak in configuration and data models. The BA converts one language into the other without losing meaning, and challenges both sides when what they ask for is not what they need.

Trust is earned by asking "why" three times. When Greg Nweshi, CEO of the fictional BrightLogistics freight brokerage, says leads are slow to dispatch, the first "why" surfaces that inbound web leads sit in a shared email inbox. The second reveals that only the dispatcher on the 8 a.m. shift reads that inbox. The third exposes the root cause: there is no automatic assignment mechanism. Root causes, not symptoms, become requirements — "assign every inbound lead to a dispatcher within 60 seconds" is buildable; "dispatches feel slow" is not.

2. The Delivery Life Cycle and the BA's Focus in Each Phase

A project moves through six stages, and the BA's outputs change with each one — the exam rewards candidates who can name the artifact for each stage.

PhaseBA focusKey artifact
DiscoveryUnderstand goals and pain pointsInterview notes, stakeholder map
DefinitionDocument requirementsRequirement document, user stories
DesignFit-gap, solution designFit-gap matrix, wireframes
BuildExplain behavior to developersAccepted stories, clarifications
TestPlan and run UATUAT plan, test cases
DeployTrain, communicate, drive adoptionTraining plan, release notes

Early phases produce analysis, middle phases produce decisions, late phases produce evidence. A stakeholder map and agreed discovery notes end Discovery; a signed-off requirement document closes Definition; a passed UAT script closes Test. Each artifact feeds the next: the map feeds the requirement document, which feeds the test cases.

3. Discovery: Understand Goals and Pain Points

Discovery answers two questions: what problem are we solving, and for whom? You run structured interviews, observe real work, and read the reports stakeholders already produce. BrightLogistics is the textbook case: 40 employees run a freight brokerage on Excel and email, and inbound web leads sit unread for one to two days before a dispatcher touches them. Here the project KPI is set: cut the lead-to-dispatch cycle from roughly 48 hours to under 4, and auto-assign at least 80% of inbound leads without human re-entry within 60 days of go-live.

4. Definition: Document Requirements

Definition is where the "what" becomes formal. You write functional and non-functional requirements, structure them into a Business Requirements Document (BRD), and prioritize them with MoSCoW. A BrightLogistics requirement such as "route each inbound web lead to exactly one open dispatcher list" is a Definition artifact, and so is its non-functional sibling "the routing decision must complete in under 5 seconds for 50 concurrent submissions."

Every requirement is numbered, independent, and testable. Numbering matters because User Story Creation (18% of the exam) treats a requirement as the parent of user stories, and Requirements Elicitation (18%) treats it as the thing that must be traceable to a source and to UAT test cases. In this lab the requirement lives on Business_Requirement__c, whose Status__c tracks Draft, In Review, Approved, Implemented, Verified, and Rejected — definitions live in force-app/main/default/objects/Business_Requirement__c/. The approval journey is captured by the Requirement_Approval_Routing Flow and an approval process on the same object, studied in Phase 4.

5. Design: Fit-Gap and Solution Decisions

Design answers "how, and with what?" The BA builds a fit-gap matrix comparing each requirement against out-of-the-box platform capability. Configure-first is the default: standard objects, fields, validation rules, and Flows cover most needs without code. Uncovered requirements become a decision to build, buy an AppExchange package, or adjust the requirement.

Two mistakes are common. First, "portal" is generic: a portal-to-submit-cases ask may be satisfied by Experience Cloud, a Salesforce site, or a public form plus List View — explore configure-first, then AppExchange, then custom code. Second, forgetting that a wireframe reviewed now costs minutes, while the same misunderstanding found in UAT costs a sprint. The BrightLogistics to-be design — Web-to-Lead capture, assignment rules, a dispatch dashboard — picks platform-native machinery at every step.

6. Build: Keep the Developers Honest

During build the BA is the team's memory of the business. Developers implement configuration and Apex; the BA explains behavior, answers clarifications, and confirms that what is built still matches what was written. This is when tolerated ambiguity resurfaces — the developer who asks "which record type does a web lead get when State is blank?" exposes a gap that should have been a default or validation rule.

The lab supports this with seven triggers that delegate logic to service classes: BusinessRequirementTrigger in force-app/main/default/triggers/ hands context to RequirementsTraceabilityService. The trigger-light, service-heavy pattern mirrors the analyst's own discipline — one source of truth, small focused units. Accepted stories and clarifications, never new requirements, are the artifacts of build.

7. Test: Plan and Run UAT

User Acceptance Testing (UAT) is where the delivered solution meets the business's own test cases. The BA plans the sessions, writes test cases derived from requirements, invites the right stakeholders, and logs defects when behavior deviates. A UAT test case on UAT_Test_Case__c carries Status__c, Severity__c, and Signed_Off__c and hangs off its parent User_Story__c — the chain is Requirement to Story to Test Case.

For BrightLogistics the killer UAT scenario is inbound lead flow: submit the web form, confirm the Lead record appears within seconds, confirm the dispatcher owner is auto-assigned, confirm no retyping. UAT confirms the business need is met, not a bug hunt. A failed test is a defect, a change request, or a data issue, routed with the UATDefectLoggerService pattern in Phase 12.

8. Deploy: Train, Communicate, Adopt

Deployment is where good analysis meets reality. The BA writes release notes, builds the training plan, and drives adoption once real records flow. Dispatchers will not trust a routing engine on day one unless someone has shown them what an assignment looks like and what to do with a blank lead.

Adoption metrics matter: sixty days after go-live the project is judged on whether 80% of inbound leads were auto-assigned without re-entry — a number the BA influences through training, communication, and a feedback loop that turns complaints into backlog items. The discipline that keeps users engaged is covered in Phase 13, and ChangeManagementService in force-app/main/default/classes/ models adoption metrics as reportable Cases.

9. The Salesforce Ecosystem: A Multi-Tenant Cloud Platform

Salesforce is a multi-tenant cloud: many customers share infrastructure while each sees an isolated environment, with data, metadata, and security partitioned. That design is why the platform upgrades three times a year and why configuration from API version 68.0 keeps working.

The ecosystem is organized around core clouds: Sales Cloud for leads, opportunities, and pipeline; Service Cloud for cases; Marketing Cloud for journeys; Experience Cloud for communities. A BA must be literate in all four because the same stakeholder word — "portal", "case", "campaign" — means different things in each cloud. BrightLogistics touches Sales Cloud for leads and will likely draw in Experience Cloud the day Greg asks for a customer tracking page, since a freight brokerage dispatches for clients who want visibility.

10. Standard Objects, Custom Objects, and the Data Model

Standard objects — Account, Contact, Lead, Opportunity, Case — cover the common CRM domain every business shares. They are a starting point, not a limitation: the Lead object natively captures inbound inquiry, Web-to-Lead fills it, and assignment rules route it before a single custom element is drawn.

Custom objects, whose API names end in __c, extend the model to your unique nouns. The lab defines Business_Requirement__c, User_Story__c, Stakeholder__c, UAT_Test_Case__c, Process_Map__c, and Training_Question__c under force-app/main/default/objects/. These are not classic business-domain objects — they are the BA's own working artifacts, the data trail of the analysis. Whether a noun becomes a standard object, a custom object, or just a field is the heart of data modeling, covered in Phase 5.

11. The Declarative Toolkit: Flows, Approvals, Reports

Most business needs are met without code. The toolkit every BA must know: validation rules guard data quality at entry; Flows capture multi-step automation; approval processes gate decisions by routing records to approvers; reports and dashboards turn the data model into decisions.

The lab models each pattern with a working example. The Requirement_Approval_Routing Flow (force-app/main/default/flows/) submits Business_Requirement__c to its approval process (force-app/main/default/approvalProcesses/) and publishes the Requirement_Status_Changed__e platform event on approval. That is the automation a BA specifies in requirements: not "build an integration" but "when a requirement is approved, notify its submitter and unpark connected stories."

12. The Platform Funnel and the Artifacts a BA Produces

Memorize the platform funnel: Requirements, Data Model, Automation, Interface, Reporting. A stakeholder asking for "a dashboard of dispatch times" forces you to notice the data model has no stored dispatch timestamp yet — the requirement comes first.

text
Requirements -> Data Model -> Automation -> Interface -> Reporting

The artifacts mirror the funnel: the requirement document feeds the data dictionary, which feeds the Flows spec, which feeds wireframes, which feed report requirements. In this lab the trail is real: Business_Requirement__c, the Flows in force-app/main/default/flows/, the dashboard and two reports, and the Business_Analyst.permissionset-meta.xml permission set. Deploy with sf project deploy start --source-dir force-app/main/default --target-org myDevOrg and verify the learning objects with BusinessAnalystFundamentalsTest in force-app/main/default/classes/.

13. The CBA Exam Blueprint and the 17-Phase Roadmap

The CBA exam has six weighted knowledge areas: Customer Discovery (17%), Collaboration and Communication (23%), Business Process Mapping (12%), Requirements Elicitation (18%), User Story Creation (18%), and Development Support and User Acceptance (12%). Sixty scored questions plus up to five unscored run in 105 minutes at a 72% pass bar; the exam costs $200 plus tax with a $100 retake. The roadmap assigns Discovery and collaboration to Phases 1-2, Business Process Mapping to Phase 3, Requirements Elicitation to Phases 4 and 11, User Story Creation to Phase 6, and Development Support and UAT to Phases 9 and 12. The facts are also stored in Certification_Setting__mdt, which Phase 14 drills you on.

You need not memorize the percentages, but the weights map where the profession spends its energy. Collaboration at 23% confirms interviews and stakeholder management are the largest slice of the job — which is why the first three phases are pure people-and-process work, and platform mechanics arrive only once the analysis discipline is in place.

Hands-On Exercises

Exercise 1.1: The Five-Why Drill on BrightLogistics Lead Intake

  1. Take the symptom: "leads take 1-2 days to be dispatched."
  2. Ask "why" against the BrightLogistics facts (leads arrive via a web form into an email inbox; one dispatcher reads it), recording each answer as a statement.
  3. Repeat until you reach a root cause stated as a fact about the environment, not a guess.
  4. Convert the root cause into one measurable requirement sentence containing "must".

Expected result: a five-why chain ending at "no automated assignment exists" plus a buildable requirement like "inbound web leads must be auto-assigned to a dispatcher within 60 seconds." What it proves: root causes, not symptoms, produce testable requirements. Pairs with Exercise 1.2 Root-cause analysis in Phase 15.

Exercise 1.2: Artifact-to-Phase Matching Game

  1. Write the six life cycle phases on cards, and the six key artifacts on another set, shuffled.
  2. Match each artifact to its phase, then name the artifact that ends Discovery.
  3. Repeat for StudyBuddy Tutoring: what would Discovery produce for an agency keeping tutor availability in a spreadsheet?

Expected result: a correct artifact-to-phase table for both businesses and a confident answer that a stakeholder map and discovery notes close Discovery. What it proves: which stage each BA output belongs to. Pairs with Exercise 1.5 Artifact matching in Phase 15.

Exercise 1.3: Platform Funnel Walkthrough

  1. Pick the ask: "I want to see today's dispatch times at a glance."
  2. Apply the funnel Requirements, Data Model, Automation, Interface, Reporting top to bottom, writing what BrightLogistics is missing at each stage (e.g., Data Model: no stored dispatch timestamp).
  3. Present the funnel as a numbered gap list with the object or feature that fills each gap.

Expected result: a five-row table linking each funnel stage to a concrete missing piece and the object or feature that fills it. What it proves: you design solutions backward from their data and reporting needs. Pairs with Exercise 1.3 Ecosystem scavenger hunt in Phase 15.

Key Terms Glossary

TermDefinition
Business Analyst (BA)The professional who bridges business needs and technical delivery by eliciting, documenting, and verifying requirements.
Delivery life cycleThe six project stages Discovery, Definition, Design, Build, Test, Deploy, each with its BA artifact.
Multi-tenant architectureA cloud model where customers share infrastructure but each has isolated data, metadata, and security.
Standard objectAn out-of-the-box Salesforce object such as Account, Contact, Lead, Opportunity, or Case.
Custom objectAn org-defined object whose API name ends in __c, extending the model to business-specific nouns.
Declarative developmentBuilding on the platform through clicks, configuration, and metadata rather than programmatic code.
FlowA declarative tool that automates business processes with steps, decisions, and actions.
Approval processA routed, formal sign-off of a record gated by approvers and notifications.
Platform funnelThe analytical order Requirements, Data Model, Automation, Interface, Reporting used to design solutions.
ArtifactA tangible BA output such as a stakeholder map, BRD, fit-gap matrix, UAT plan, or release note.
CBA blueprintThe six weighted knowledge areas that make up the Salesforce Certified Business Analyst exam.
Fit-gap matrixA comparison of each requirement against out-of-the-box platform capabilities.

Certification Checkpoints

  • I can name the six delivery life cycle phases and the artifact that ends each one.
  • I can explain what a Salesforce BA does during Discovery, Build, and UAT.
  • I can sketch the platform funnel and walk any stakeholder ask through it.
  • I can name the six CBA blueprint areas, their weights, and the exam format facts (60 scored + up to 5 unscored, 105 minutes, 72% pass, $200, $100 retake).
  • I can state the BrightLogistics problem and KPI.
  • I can locate at least three BA artifacts in the force-app folder.

Summary

You have defined what a Salesforce Business Analyst actually does — translate, document, validate, and verify — and tracked that work through a six-stage delivery life cycle from Discovery to Deploy. You mapped the Salesforce ecosystem and its declarative toolkit, learned the platform funnel that turns requirements into data models, automation, interfaces, and reporting, and connected every BA artifact to the six knowledge areas of the CBA exam. The BrightLogistics CRM rollout and its lead-to-dispatch KPI will now follow you through the roadmap as the running case study on which every later skill is practiced.
